3. Shareholder action: owners use their votes and voice (agenda items, coordinated voting, campaigns, proxy contests).
4. Regulation: the state sets rules that make monitoring easier (SOX, Dodd-Frank).
Trap: Calling a pay change 'monitoring' because the board decides it. Nobody watches the CEO more closely; his incentives change.
(lecture 13 p. 3)

front: According to Kurbatov, who can monitor the managers of a firm and with what?
back:
Shareholders (especially big institutions) and the board; to a degree also lenders, employees, authorities and outsiders
1. Shareholders, above all large institutions: votes, proposals, engagement, proxy fights.
2. The board: hires, fires and pays the executives and takes the major decisions.
3. Lenders: covenants and the threat of calling the loan. Employees: they see problems first and can blow the whistle. Authorities: fraud cases.
4. External monitoring: the market for corporate control (the threat of a takeover), analysts and the press.
Trap: Listing small dispersed shareholders as monitors: each keeps too little of the gain to pay the cost, so they free-ride.
(lecture 13 p. 4, lecture 14 p. 24)

front: What makes a board good or bad at monitoring? Use Kurbatov's list.
back:
Independence above all; watch for captive boards, a CEO as chair, staggered terms, size and busy directors
1. Directors can be insiders (employees), gray (ties to the firm, such as its lawyer or banker) or independent. Independent boards monitor better.
2. A captive board was picked by the CEO it should watch. A CEO who chairs the board sets its agenda.
3. A staggered board elects only some seats each year, which makes incumbents much harder to replace.
4. Size and time: a large board coordinates poorly. Directors with many seats are too busy to monitor.
Trap: Counting gray directors as independent; treating a board as independent because it has a majority of outsiders while the CEO chairs it.
(lecture 13 p. 5, manual 27.2)

front: A board has 9 seats with staggered three-year terms (3 seats elected each year). An activist wants a majority to replace the CEO. How many annual meetings does it need, even if it wins every contested seat?
back:
Two meetings
1. A majority of 9 is 5 seats.
2. First meeting: 3 seats, short of 5.
3. Second meeting: 6 seats, a majority.
4. That delay is why Kurbatov calls a staggered board 'much harder to replace incumbent members'. It is also why it works as a takeover defence.
Trap: One meeting (forgetting that only a third of the seats are up); three (thinking every seat must be replaced).
(lecture 13 p. 5, sjangre governance-4)

front: A firm earns 500 a year, including 40 of interest on 1 000 of cash (4%). It has 200 shares at 50; no taxes, perfect markets. The CEO's bonus depends on EPS. He spends all the cash buying back shares at 50. What happens to EPS and to the share price?
back:
EPS rises from 2.5000 to 2.5556; the price stays at 50
1. Shares bought: 1 000/50 = 20, leaving 180.
2. Earnings lose the interest: 500 − 40 = 460. EPS = 460/180 = 2.5556.
3. Equity was 200 × 50 = 10 000; 1 000 is paid out; 9 000/180 = 50. Owners gain nothing.
4. Kurbatov's point: KPI targets make managers short-sighted. They may prefer such moves, or cut long-term projects, to hit this year's number.
Trap: 'EPS is up, so value is up.' The buyback moves cash from the firm to the sellers at a fair price; the bonus pays for nothing.
(lecture 14 recording, lecture 13 p. 7)

front: Can you design a perfect pay contract for a CEO? Discuss performance metrics, stock-based pay and golden parachutes.
back:
No: every tool fixes one problem and creates another
1. Performance metrics (EPS, KPIs): easy to observe, but the manager targets the number rather than the value. He becomes short-sighted.
2. Stock-based pay: ties his wealth to the share price, but short vesting invites timing and options can reward risk taking. Use long vesting and clawbacks.
3. Golden parachutes: can stop a CEO from blocking a good takeover to save his job, but can also reward failure or buy his consent to a low offer.
4. Monitor too hard and the manager becomes too passive; give him freedom and he may shirk. That is the trade-off.
Trap: Claiming more stock-based pay always aligns interests. It aligns him with the share price, which he can move in the short run.
(lecture 13 p. 6 to 7 and 15)

front: A firm is worth 2 000 million. Active monitoring costs 2 million a year and would raise the value by 2%. Does a 7% owner monitor? A 0.1% owner?
back:
The 7% owner does (2.8 > 2); the 0.1% owner does not (0.04 < 2)
1. Value created: 2% × 2 000 = 40 million.
2. 7% owner keeps 0.07 × 40 = 2.8 > 2: monitoring pays.
3. 0.1% owner keeps 0.001 × 40 = 0.04 < 2: he free-rides.
4. Rule: monitor if α × ΔV > C. This is why large holders and institutions monitor and dispersed owners do not.
Trap: Comparing the full 40 with the cost: everyone gains from monitoring, but each pays the whole cost alone.
(manual 27.1, H2025 E2)

front: What can shareholders do, beyond selling? List Kurbatov's forms of shareholder action.
back:
'Just vote no', agenda items, coordinated voting, activist campaigns, proxy contests
1. 'Just vote no': vote against directors or the pay plan. It rarely wins outright, but a large protest vote is a signal.
2. Add items to the agenda of the meeting (shareholder proposals).
3. Coordinated voting: institutions vote together.
4. Activist campaigns: public letters and plans. Proxy contests: run your own slate of directors.
5. Facts from the readings: retail investors vote little. Institutions often delegate to proxy advisers.
Trap: Treating exit (selling) as monitoring. It can discipline through the share price, but it gives up the voice.
(lecture 13 p. 8)

front: Many funds vote as the proxy adviser ISS or Glass Lewis recommends. Is that optimal?
back:
Cheap but not obviously optimal: one standard policy replaces judgment at each firm
1. A fund with small stakes in thousands of firms would spend more on research than it gains at each one (α × ΔV < C), so buying a recommendation is rational.
2. The cost of research is shared across all the adviser's clients.
3. But votes follow a template rather than the facts at each firm. Advisers also gain influence without owning anything or bearing the consequences.
4. Kurbatov's question 'is that optimal?' wants both sides.
Trap: Saying advisers solve the free-rider problem completely, or that they hold the shares themselves.
(lecture 13 p. 9)

front: A new board demands approval for every project and says it will fire the CEO after one loss-making quarter. What is the likely effect on firm value?
back:
Probably lower: the CEO becomes too passive and drops risky positive-NPV projects
1. A risky project with positive NPV can lose money in some quarter. The CEO now bears that risk with his job; the owners keep the upside.
2. He picks safe, low-value projects instead.
3. Kurbatov: 'a manager who is monitored too strongly will be too passive'. The trade-off is freedom for the manager or tight control.
4. Entrenchment is the opposite failure: a manager protected by a staggered board or defences is monitored too little.
Trap: 'More monitoring always means more value.' Past some point it buys less shirking at the price of less risk taking.
(lecture 13 p. 15 and 18)

front: What did Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank change in corporate governance? Why did they come?
back:
SOX: independent auditors, more disclosure, personal responsibility. Dodd-Frank: independent pay committees, nominations by large holders
1. Background: the frauds of the early 2000s, with Enron (about 11 billion dollars of shareholder losses) as the landmark case. Earlier, the 1984 Insider Trading Sanctions Act targeted insiders.
2. Sarbanes-Oxley: independent auditors, enhanced disclosure, corporate responsibility for the accounts.
3. Dodd-Frank (after the financial crisis): many stability rules, plus independent compensation committees and a right for large shareholders to nominate board members.
4. Regulation supports monitoring; it does not replace it.
Trap: Swapping the two acts. SOX is about the numbers; Dodd-Frank strengthened shareholders against the board.
(lecture 13 p. 17)

front: Shareholders or stakeholders? A CEO keeps an unprofitable plant open to protect local jobs. Discuss.
back:
Friedman: the CEO spends the owners' money on a goal they did not choose. The counterargument: firms have many constituencies
1. Friedman (1970): the manager is the owners' agent. Social goals are for owners to fund with their own money if they want them.
2. Kurbatov's worry about the stakeholder view: too many missions and conflicting interests make the manager accountable to no one.
3. The other side: CSR and the Stanford survey. 89% of executives call stakeholders important and only 23% say shareholders clearly come first; employees are ranked most important.
4. A balanced answer: stakeholder care that raises long-run value is consistent with value maximisation; spending that does not is an agency cost.
Trap: Using the survey as proof that the plant should stay open. It describes what CEOs believe, not whose money it is.
(lecture 1 p. 28 to 32, lecture 13 p. 2)

front: A mature firm generates 400 a year of free cash flow and has no positive-NPV projects. The CEO, who owns 0.2% of the shares, wants to reinvest it all to grow. What are the four uses of free cash flow? Which is best here?
back:
Dividend, buyback, hold cash, reinvest. Pay it out: reinvesting here is empire building
1. Under MM the choice is irrelevant. With frictions it is not.
2. Without positive-NPV projects, every reinvestment has a negative NPV: a bigger firm worth less.
3. The CEO bears 0.2% of the loss but enjoys all of the size and prestige: the agency problem in miniature.
4. Dividends or buybacks take the cash out of his hands. Dividends are sticky (cutting them is punished); buybacks are flexible and can signal undervaluation.
Trap: 'Under MM it does not matter.' The question is about agency, where it does.
(lecture 14 recording, lecture 5)

front: Why can an LBO or a takeover threat work as governance?
back:
It replaces or disciplines management from outside the firm
1. A badly run firm trades below what it would be worth under good managers. A bidder or LBO fund can buy it, replace the managers and keep the gain.
2. In an LBO the new owners hold a large stake (no free-rider problem) and the heavy debt commits the managers to pay out cash instead of building empires.
3. Even the threat of a bid disciplines current managers, which is why defences that remove the threat are a governance concern.
Trap: Treating the market for corporate control as a monitor with daily tools. It works through the threat and the occasional bid.
(manual 27.6, lecture 12 p. 11)

front: A governance question names no country. Which framework do you answer in? When do you bring in Norwegian company law?
back:
Answer in the general (Kurbatov's) framework; bring in Norwegian law only if the question says ASA or Norway
1. Kurbatov teaches governance in a general, largely American frame: boards, staggered boards, proxy fights, ISS, SOX, Dodd-Frank.
2. H2024 E2 and H2025 E2 name no jurisdiction. The keys accept any reasonable mechanism with an explanation.
3. If the case is a Norwegian ASA, one sentence on the general meeting or the board's duties can add precision, but it does not replace the mechanism.
Trap: Building the answer on Norwegian law, or calling an American mechanism 'wrong' because Norwegian law differs. The points are for mechanisms, tools and who uses them.
(lecture 13, docs forelesninger A7)

front: What does Kurbatov's exam look like? Structure, points, time and grading.
back:
Exactly as H2024 and H2025: two theory questions, four problems, every block covered
1. Two theory questions of about 10 to 12 points each, answerable with sound reasoning; four computational problems, about 80% of the paper, several ending with 3 to 5 points of intuition.
2. Every block gets at least one exercise or sub-question: capital structure and payout, valuation with leverage, options and real options, M&A and governance.
3. Part (a) is easy. No multiple choice. The formula sheet is the last page; your own sheets are not allowed. Calculator (ideally scientific with powers) and one bilingual dictionary.
4. Three or four hours: check the exam information. Graded on a curve by examiners; the A line has been about 90 to 91 points.
Trap: Preparing from pre-2024 exams as if they were his: 2022 is close and 2016 only with care. Their M&A and governance parts are not representative.
(lecture 14 recording)

front: How do you budget time across the six exercises?
back:
About 1.6 minutes per point on a 3-hour paper, 2.2 on a 4-hour one, with a stop time written next to each exercise
1. Spend the first 10 minutes reading every exercise and writing the points next to each.
2. Three hours: 180 − 10 reading − 10 checking = 160 minutes for 100 points, 1.6 a point. A 12-point exercise gets about 19 minutes, a 20-point one about 32.
3. Four hours: 240 − 10 − 10 = 220 minutes, 2.2 a point. A 12-point exercise gets about 26 minutes, a 20-point one 44.
4. Write the closing minute in the margin. When the clock passes it, move on and come back later.
5. Early sub-questions are the easy ones, so a started exercise beats perfecting a hard part.
Trap: Starting with the biggest exercise and reaching minute 150 with both theory questions unwritten.
(manual 28.1)

front: The question says 'evaluate the project'. You have the firm's levered value and the project's PV. What do you report?
back:
The project's NPV: its PV minus its investment, not the firm's value
1. Kurbatov: 'if it says evaluate the project, I want the NPV of the project, not the firm'. Reporting firm value costs a lot of points.
2. PV is not NPV: subtract the investment before you report.
3. Underline 'project' or 'firm' and 'PV' or 'NPV' in the question before you compute.
Trap: Firm value reported as the answer, or a PV with the investment never subtracted.
(lecture 14 recording, manual 28.7)

front: How many decimals? When do you round?
back:
Typically four decimals, at most four for small numbers; round only when you write the final number
1. Kurbatov: typically four decimals, at most four for small numbers; no cents when the numbers are in billions.
2. H2025 E4: 'Recommended precision is 4 decimal places (as in, 1.2345 instead of 1.23)', for amounts such as 72.0178 as well as for rates.
3. Carry six decimals inside a chain. A rate rounded early moves a perpetuity by whole units and spreads through every later step.
Trap: Rounding ρ, a monthly rate or a discount factor mid-chain, or reporting small amounts with two decimals. The H2025 key accepts a drift of about 0.001 but calls about 0.05 too much.
(lecture 14 recording, H2025 E4, manual 28.7)

front: You cannot get part (b), but parts (c) and (d) build on it. What do you do?
back:
Name the missing number as a symbol or a labelled assumption and carry on: follow-on errors are not punished twice
1. Kurbatov: a later part that uses your wrong earlier number correctly gets full marks.
2. Write 'I could not obtain βU in (b); I carry it forward as βU' and do the algebra.
3. If a number is needed, assume one and label it: 'Assume βU = 1.4, since (b) is unresolved.'
4. Leave nothing blank: an empty sub-question is the only guaranteed zero.
Trap: Stopping at the broken part, or inventing a number silently, which makes later parts look wrong rather than consistent.
(lecture 14 recording, manual 28.8)

front: Which discount rate goes with which valuation method? And why is r_wacc below r_U?
back:
FCFE at rE, APV at rU, WACC method at rwacc
1. Given rwacc: expect the WACC method. Given rU: expect APV. Maybe both: then they must agree.
2. FCF never subtracts interest; the tax benefit of debt enters through rwacc or through PV(TS), never twice. FCFE = FCF − (1 − τ) × interest + net borrowing, discounted at rE.
3. rwacc = rU − (D/V)τrD under constant leverage: the after-tax cost of debt carries the tax shield, so rwacc is below rU whenever there is debt and tax. Example: 10% − 0.4 × 0.22 × 5% = 9.56%.
Trap: Discounting FCF at rE, subtracting interest from FCF and then also using rwacc (tax shield counted twice).
(lecture 14 recording, lecture 14 p. 16 to 18)

front: The annual rate is 8%. What do you use for 6 months, for 18 months and for one month?
back:
6 months: 3.9230%. 18 months: factor 1.081.5 = 1.122369. One month: 0.6434%
1. Compound, never divide: (1 + r)T with T in years.
2. Six months: √1.08 − 1 = 3.9230%.
3. 18 months: discount with 1.081.5 = 1.122369. This is how Kurbatov annualises Google's 18-month yield.
4. Monthly: 1.081/12 − 1 = 0.6434%; back again (1 + rm)12 − 1 = 8%.
Trap: 8%/2 = 4% and 8%/12 = 0.6667%. Kurbatov said he would not be surprised to see this on the exam.
(lecture 14 recording, manual 28.7)

front: Read what is asked: which small words in a question change the answer you must give?
back:
'Most you would pay', 'from today's perspective', 'as perceived by the market', 'answer both questions', 'actual premium'
1. 'How much would you pay': a maximum, the value of the information or option, not a price.
2. 'NPV from today's perspective': discount date-1 values back to date 0.
3. 'Probability as perceived by the market': a risk-neutral (or rf-discounted) probability backed out of prices.
4. 'Answer both questions': two answers, each stated in words. H2025 E1 said it outright: 'Please be very clear and answer both questions'.
5. 'Offered' or 'actual' premium; 'stand-alone' or 'combined'; 'value of the option' (against the best alternative, which is often 0).
Trap: Answering a nearby question correctly. The key gives no points for the number that was not asked.
(lecture 14 recording, manual 28.7)

front: How do you write a 12-point verbal answer (governance or M&A motives)?
back:
Exactly the number of items asked, each in its own paragraph: the mechanism named first, then who, how and why, within the sentence budget
1. Count the items: 'two methods', 'three actions', 'four boxes'. Each is graded on its own, so three solid items beat one brilliant one.
2. First line of each item: the name of the mechanism ('the board', 'disciplinary takeover', 'winner's curse').
3. Then explain it with the case facts (the 5 to 10% stake, the price reaction).
4. Keep to the budget: 2 to 3 or 3 to 4 sentences. Length is not rewarded.
Trap: Overlapping items, items without a mechanism, a general essay on governance, or synergies when they are banned.
(manual 28.5, H2024 E1 and E2, H2025 E2)

front: The exam asks about Black-Scholes. What will you have to do? What not?
back:
No Black-Scholes calculation; explain directions and mechanisms
1. Kurbatov, repeatedly: 'Black-Scholes calculation will not be in the exam. Intuition can be there.' You need not explain N(d1).
2. Expect: what a change in σ, T, rf, S or K does to a call or a put and why; implied against true volatility (H2025 E1); American against European.
3. Option prices you must compute come from parity or the binomial model.
4. No American options to price, only the intuition.
Trap: Spending exam minutes computing d1 and N(d1). It earns nothing and costs time.
(lecture 14 recording)

front: A strategy costs 100 today and pays 108.15 or 78.15 in a year (rf = 3%). Which equation gives the implied probability? What error do the keys name here?
back:
100 × 1.03 = p × 108.15 + (1 − p) × 78.15, so p = 0.8283
1. Move every amount to the same date before you compare. Today's 100 is worth 103 in a year.
2. 103 − 78.15 = 30p gives p = 0.8283.
3. The same habit applies everywhere: a certainty equivalent, a date-1 NPV brought back to date 0, an amount paid later in a real option.
Trap: 100 = p × 108.15 + (1 − p) × 78.15, which gives 0.7283: p comes out 10 percentage points too low, the error the H2025 key singles out.
(H2025 E6, manual 28.7)

front: Which checks close an answer? What does each catch?
back:
Run a check that can fail and write one line saying it passed
1. Valuation: WACC value = APV value; weighted betas (E/V)βE + (D/V)βD = βU.
2. Agency: creditors' gain + shareholders' gain = the project's NPV; with fixed total value, one side's gain is the other's loss.
3. Options: ρ between 0 and 1; parity C − P = S − PV(K); D + E = V; a second twin for the same stream gives the same ρ.
4. Real options: the option's value equals the probability of the branch it changes times the improvement there, discounted.
5. M&A: the NPVs to acquirer and target sum to S; the long-short route and the spread shortcut give the same p.
Trap: Running a check that is an identity by construction and believing it tests the inputs: ρ always reprices the S0 it came from; p always reprices the outlay. Those lines only confirm the arithmetic.
(manual 28.6)

front: Which words in a question tell you which method to use?
back:
Match the cue to the routine before you touch the numbers
1. 'Assume perfect capital markets': MM; show that debt and equity give the same value.
2. 'Uncorrelated with the market', 'the probability is known': real probabilities discounted at rf.
3. 'You do not know the probabilities', 'traded price', 'up and down': risk-neutral ρ from the twin.
4. 'Maintains a target D/E': tax shield at rU. 'Permanent debt of X': tax shield at rD, PV(TS) = τD.
5. 'Invest now or wait', 'may exit': fold the tree back, max at each node, compare with 0.
Trap: Choosing the method from the topic heading instead of from the wording. The paper gives no headings.
(lecture 14 recording, manual 28.2)

front: What is on the formula sheet? What must you know by heart for blocks 3 and 4?
back:
On the sheet: binomial replication and ρ, the stock-swap NPVs and the exchange-ratio cap. By heart: everything else in options, real options and deal probabilities
1. On the sheet: Δ, B and ρ = [(1 + rf)S0 − Sd]/(Su − Sd); the M&A swap NPVs and ER = x/NT ≤ [(T + S)/A](NA/NT). Nothing else from blocks 3 and 4.
2. By heart: put-call parity C + PV(K) = P + S; E = C(K) and D = PV(K) − P(K); senior and junior debt from calls; the CDS from ρ.
3. By heart: everything about real options (max at each node, value of information, exit as a put, compare with 0).
4. By heart: cash NPVs S − (P − T) and P − T; the deal probability from the long-short position with (1 + rf)T.
Trap: Assuming parity or the deal-probability set-up will be printed. Write the unprinted formulas on scrap paper in the first minute.
(formula sheet, manual 28.7)

front: Kurbatov said decision trees help but are unlikely to earn points by themselves. How should you use one in a real-option answer?
back:
As a tool: maximum at each decision node first, then probability-weight and discount. Report the option as a difference
1. Squares for decisions, circles for chance, numbers on every branch.
2. At each decision node take max(continue, stop, 0) before averaging; averaging first erases the option.
3. Report the option's value as the difference between two strategies you have both computed.
4. Compare with the best alternative, which is often doing nothing (0), not a negative NPV.
Trap: A beautiful tree with no numbers or no conclusion. Points are for values and the decision in words ('wait', 'open').
(lecture 14 recording, manual 25.7)

front: How should you prepare in the last weeks, according to Kurbatov?
back:
His two exams, then the problem sets, then the slides; the textbook last
1. H2024 and H2025: same structure and spirit, not identical questions.
2. Problem sets: anything solvable in a few lines can come, often with a twist; big Excel exercises will not. The stars say nothing about difficulty.
3. The M&A lecture is Problem Set 4 (the 'minus one' example and the three at the end). Governance has no computations.
4. Slides: 'understand everything in this presentation, preferably in all the presentations'. Textbook chapters and exercises have lower priority.
Trap: Treating pre-2024 exams as his. M&A and governance there are not representative.
(lecture 14 recording)
